extracted.intended_audience: parents/guardians and tutors of young gentlemen (aristocratic families)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical guidance for selecting a governor/tutor and shaping the upbringing, studies, manners, and bodily training of a boy of quality so he becomes a wise, virtuous, and capable man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a 'well-made' head over a 'well-filled' one
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a tutor who has good manners and judgment rather than merely extensive book-learning (‘Tete bien faite’). Seek both, but prefer the former for a boy meant to be an accomplished cavalier rather than a mere scholar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: ‘seeking, indeed, both the one and the other, but rather of the two to prefer manners and judgment to mere learning.’ Servan note: 'Tete bien faite' (expression created by Montaigne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a conversational/Socratic method (let the pupil speak)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tutor should not simply pour information into the pupil’s ear; he should permit the pupil to taste things himself, speak in turn, be tested, and sometimes be left to open the way for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Socrates and Arcesilaus: make scholars speak first, then instruct. Anti-pattern: the funnel method of rote lecturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor instruction to the pupil's capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not teach several boys of differing capacities with one identical lesson and measure; adjust teaching to individual vigour and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Such as...undertake, with one and the same lesson...to instruct several boys of differing and unequal capacities, are infinitely mistaken.’ Emphasize proportional adjustment and condescension to pupil's motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge learning by practical application, not memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess progress by how the pupil applies what he has learned in life, not by his ability to repeat words from memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the master examine 'about the sense' of lessons and make the pupil put learning into a hundred different forms and subjects (Plato's pedagogic institutions). Rote repetition = 'no knowledge'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require active reworking and application of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the pupil rephrase and accommodate learning to many subjects to ensure understanding—knowledge should be transformed, not disgorged in the same condition it was swallowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor of digestion: the mind must 'alter the form and condition' of received material. Make him put what he has learned into 'a hundred several forms'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach critical thinking and independent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the pupil examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads; nothing should be lodged upon mere authority or trust; present diverse opinions so he may choose or remain in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's principles must not be accepted as final; expose Epicurean, Stoic, Platonic views. Encourage 'I love to doubt, as well as to know' (Dante).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internalize knowledge so it becomes one's own judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The pupil should 'imbibe' knowledge and transform borrowed fragments into his own work and judgment; it matters less where materials come from than what he makes of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bees metaphor: gather sweets from many flowers then make one's own honey. Anti-pattern: living upon pillage and borrowing—exposed purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use daily life and practical activities as material for study
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat everyday incidents (a page’s trick, a servant’s mistake, a jest) as legitimate and fruitful subjects of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practice in concrete arts: riding, fencing, handling a pike, touching a lute—learning must involve doing, not just watching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage travel and conversation to broaden understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Send the pupil to converse with men and travel abroad to learn humours, manners, customs, and laws and to sharpen his wit by rubbing against others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel not for trivial accounts of monuments but to report manners; travel young to acquire foreign tongues before the tongue stiffens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send the boy abroad early for language acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the pupil in neighboring nations whose language differs from his own while he is young so his tongue remains flexible to learn it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit: 'I would that a boy should be sent abroad very young...into those neighbouring nations whose language is most differing from our own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overindulgent maternal upbringing; toughen body and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not raise a child solely in his mother's lap; mothers' tenderness can prevent necessary correction and exposure to hardships needed to make body and soul fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mothers may spare him from returning 'all dust and sweat' or from physical exercises; the child must be inured to cold drink when hot, riding unruly horses, and physical dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen the body alongside the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortify sinews and bodily constitution—labour hardens against pain and the soul is assisted by a strong body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and admission: bodily toughness is not the same as magnanimity; nevertheless a tender body makes the soul's tasks harder—train through exercise and exposure to discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accustom the pupil to endure labour and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Break a boy into toil and rough exercise so he may be trained to suffer dislocations, sickness, cauteries, imprisonment or worse; be prepared for misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare him for civil maladies; anti-pattern: overprotecting that leaves him unprepared for the world's rigours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the governor's sovereign authority; limit parental interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let parents' presence check or hinder the governor’s authority; respect for the tutor must be maintained and not undermined by family dynamics or knowledge of future inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family respect and awareness of estate greatness are inconveniences in tender years; maintain governor's authority to avoid spoiled discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate silence, modesty, and restraint in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Train the pupil to be sparing of his knowledge, modest, to refrain from reproving every idle saying, and not to carp at everything that displeases him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage being an 'husband of his knowledge'; anti-pattern: seeking reputation by interrupting or reproving others to show intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious authority and childish ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow the pupil to assume airs or privileges beyond custom; only those with great and divine gifts may safely use poetical license or exceptional behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Socrates and Aristippus as exceptions; otherwise humility and conformity to custom are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach selectivity in disputes: choose worthy opponents and fit arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruct the pupil to engage in discourse only with a champion worthy of him, to choose his reasons carefully, abominate impertinence, affect brevity, and above all to accept truth and recant when he discovers error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: engaging in every argument, using every subtlety available; value judgment and sincerity over mere clatter of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instill public duty but avoid corrupting personal ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the pupil to be a loyal subject and affectionate to his prince, but cool the desire for private ties that may blind judgment or corrupt freedom of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: purely courtly dependence corrupts freedom and causes phrase and opinion not to be trusted; seek public duty as the primary tie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make conscience and virtue evident in speech; value recantation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the pupil to speak with manifest conscience and virtue and to acknowledge errors discovered by himself—this is an effect of judgment and sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obstinacy and contention are signs of mean souls; revising one’s argument in heat of dispute is a rare and philosophical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and learn from all ranks and persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Train the pupil to have his 'eye and ear in every corner' and to examine every man's talent—from peasant to passenger—to learn something useful from all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even folly and impertinence contribute; observe graces and manners to emulate the good and despise the bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate inquisitiveness about singular and local things
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage honest curiosity: investigate any singular or rare thing near you—houses, fountains, places of battles, and also inquire into princes' manners, revenues, and alliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active curiosity sharpens judgment and furnishes knowledge useful for future occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use history to learn manners, motives, and judgment (not mere dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach history not for narrative detail (dates and events) but to extract the manners, motives, and judgments of great people—learn why actions were done, not only where or when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plutarch recommended: learn the manners of Hannibal and Scipio rather than dates. Read with care and observation to extract moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize moral philosophy and self-knowledge among liberal sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin studies with the doctrine that regulates manners and sense—teach him to know himself, what to wish, what constitutes temperance, justice, and true contentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'let us begin with that which makes us free'—limit studies to those directly serving life and virtue before abstruse branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit studies to what is truly useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid expansive, unnecessary learning; follow Socrates' counsel to focus studies where there is real utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many sciences have needless cavities and dilatations which are better left alone; teach restraint in choice of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching irrelevant abstruse knowledge early (e.g., astronomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not burden pupils with knowledge (like motions of the eighth sphere, astrology) irrelevant to their immediate life concerns when they face more pressing enemies like ambition or poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Anaximenes' objection to Pythagoras as example: prioritize pressing practical concerns over remote speculation for the young.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce formal subjects after moral formation and according to inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: After grounding in virtue and self-knowledge, present elements of logic, physics, geometry, rhetoric, and then the science the pupil is most inclined to; his formed judgment will enable choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching method should alternate discourse and reading; sometimes give whole authors, sometimes the marrow. Combine tutor with a learned man if needed to supply lacking material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh, intricate scholastic methods (Gaza); prefer clear, lively instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject precepts that are intricate, harsh, and void of vivifying content (the Gaza method); prefer material that quickens wit and fancy and that the mind can feed upon and digest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaza's precepts are 'vain, lean, and insignificant'; choose texts and methods that make the mind active and yield earlier ripeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present philosophy as cheerful and life-enhancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should be taught as an attractive, cheerful, and freeing practice—not as a grim, forbidding, or melancholy pursuit—so that it fortifies the soul with serenity and cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Demetrius story: philosophers are cheerful; the 'most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness.' Philosophy should calm storms of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach that virtue's highest value is the ease, utility, and pleasure of its exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the pupil to view true virtue as accessible, useful, and pleasurable in its practice; virtue should be acquired by order, not by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare virtuous moderation to regulating pleasures; virtue moderates and preserves pleasures rather than denying them wholly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary models (poetry and heroic figures) to shape moral imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Present heroic and active models (e.g., Bradamante, Angelica) to form natural, manly affections and to counter soft, effeminate ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By representing such heroines or heroes the pupil will choose a brave, masculine affection rather than an effeminate taste; poets accommodate themselves to public humour to instruct passions.
